title: 27.5: A 4, 100µm2 Wire-Metal-Based Temperature Sensor with a Fractional-Discharge FLL and a Time-Domain Amplifier with ±0.2°C Inaccuracy (3σ) from -40 to 125°C and 45fJ·K2 Resolution FoM in 28nm CMOS
problem: Resistance-based temperature sensors must achieve compact area (<5000µm²), high accuracy (±0.2°C, 3σ), and superior resolution FoM while operating across wide temperature ranges in advanced low-VDD processes.
motivation: Integrated temperature sensing in advanced CMOS nodes requires minimal footprint and power, supporting sub-1V operation while maintaining accuracy despite process non-idealities and transistor leakage.
method: The sensor uses a wire-metal resistor as the temperature-sensing element—as temperature changes, the resistor's resistance changes in a predictable way. A fractional-discharge FLL converts these resistance changes into changes in timing signals (by precisely controlling how long it takes to discharge a capacitor). These timing changes are then amplified by a time-domain amplifier, which detects delays instead of voltage swings, making small temperature changes measurable. This approach eliminates active biasing requirements, since passive resistors don't need the careful voltage and current control that transistor-based sensors require.
key_novelty: The key innovation is using time-domain amplification (measuring timing differences instead of voltages) combined with a fractional-discharge frequency-locking circuit and passive resistors, which achieves high accuracy without the active transistor biasing that traditional sensors require.
contributions: Passive sensing element eliminating biasing constraints
primary_theme: compact integrated resistive temperature sensor with time-domain amplification
